claim: Adult muscle precursors (AMPs) are transient fruit fly muscle stem cells that are specified during mid-embryogenesis.
source: Here, we applied a Drosophila model to follow in vivo behavior of adult muscle precursors (AMPs), the transient fruit fly muscle stem cells.
evidence: The abstract directly states that AMPs are transient fruit fly muscle stem cells, and the introduction provides additional context about their specification timing.

claim: Emerging AMPs send out thin filopodia that make contact with neighboring muscles.
source: We report that emerging AMPs send out thin filopodia that make contact with neighboring muscles.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1.

claim: AMPs maintain their filopodia-based association with muscles throughout their dormant state and when they start to proliferate.
source: AMPs keep their filopodia-based association with muscles throughout their dormant state but also when they start to proliferate, suggesting that muscles could play a role in AMP reactivation.
evidence: The abstract states this observation and Figure 3 shows AMPs maintaining connections during proliferation.

claim: Muscles send inductive dIlp6 signals that switch the Insulin pathway ON in closely associated AMPs.
source: Indeed, our genetic analyses indicate that muscles send inductive dIlp6 signals that switch the Insulin pathway ON in closely associated AMPs.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by genetic experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: Insulin pathway activation leads to the activation of Notch, which regulates AMP proliferation via dMyc.
source: This leads to the activation of Notch, which regulates AMP proliferation via dMyc.
evidence: The abstract states this cascade relationship, which is supported by genetic epistasis experiments in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Drosophila AMPs display homing behavior to muscle niche.
source: Altogether, we report that Drosophila AMPs display homing behavior to muscle niche and that the niche-driven Insulin-Notch-dMyc cascade plays a key role in setting the activated state of AMPs.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the abstract and supported by observations of filopodia dynamics and AMP-muscle interactions in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The stem cell niche was first documented in Drosophila.
source: The stem cell niche was first documented in Drosophila (Xie and Spradling, 2000) but it is now widely accepted that all adult stem cells reside within a niche that retains them and regulates their behavior (Voog and Jones, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Xie and Spradling, 2000.

claim: All adult stem cells reside within a niche that retains them and regulates their behavior.
source: The stem cell niche was first documented in Drosophila (Xie and Spradling, 2000) but it is now widely accepted that all adult stem cells reside within a niche that retains them and regulates their behavior (Voog and Jones, 2010).
evidence: This is presented as widely accepted knowledge and supported by citation to Voog and Jones, 2010.

claim: Notch signaling is required for the homing of emerging satellite cells by stimulating them to produce basal lamina.
source: It has been shown that Notch signaling is required for the homing of emerging satellite cells by stimulating them to produce basal lamina, thus promoting their adhesion to myofibers (Bröhl et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Bröhl et al., 2012.

claim: AMPs are specified at embryonic stage 12 and remain quiescent until the mid-second larval instar.
source: AMPs are specified at embryonic stage 12 and then remain quiescent and undifferentiated until the mid-second larval instar (Bate et al., 1991).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to Bate et al., 1991.

claim: Embryonic AMPs form an interconnected network via long cytoplasmic extensions soon after their specification.
source: We showed in earlier work that soon after their specification, embryonic AMPs form an interconnected network via long cytoplasmic extensions (Figeac et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to Figeac et al., 2010.

claim: Quiescent vertebrate satellite cells are connected to each other and to adjacent muscle through thin cytoplasmic extensions termed 'tunneling nanotubes'.
source: A similar feature has also been reported for the quiescent vertebrate satellite cells, which are connected to each other and to the adjacent muscle through thin cytoplasmic extensions termed 'tunneling nanotubes' (Tavi et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Tavi et al., 2010.

claim: At embryonic stage 12, AMPs appear spherical in shape and are separated from each other.
source: Initially, at embryonic stage 12, AMPs appear spherical in shape and are separated from each other (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), but a closer view (Figure 1A) shows that they send out numerous thin filopodia around their surface.
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Newly specified AMPs at stage 12 send out numerous thin filopodia around their surface.
source: Initially, at embryonic stage 12, AMPs appear spherical in shape and are separated from each other (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), but a closer view (Figure 1A) shows that they send out numerous thin filopodia around their surface.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In later embryonic stages, AMPs become more elongated and send out long cytoplasmic extensions.
source: This 'sensing behavior' also persists in later embryonic stages (Figure 1B,C), in which AMPs become more elongated and send out long cytoplasmic extensions (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) to form an interconnected network (Figeac et al., 2010).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by Figures 1B, 1C, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The long cellular processes of AMPs follow the main neural branches of the peripheral nervous system (PNS).
source: The long cellular processes follow the main neural branches of the peripheral nervous system (PNS) (Figure 1C', arrows), while the short filopodia display dynamic and irregular patterns and seem not to be attracted by the PNS nerves (Figure 1C', arrowheads).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1C'.

claim: The short filopodia of AMPs display dynamic and irregular patterns and are not attracted by PNS nerves.
source: The long cellular processes follow the main neural branches of the peripheral nervous system (PNS) (Figure 1C', arrows), while the short filopodia display dynamic and irregular patterns and seem not to be attracted by the PNS nerves (Figure 1C', arrowheads).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1C'.

claim: By embryonic stage 16, AMP filopodia had become tightly associated with neighboring muscles.
source: Our data reveal that the small filopodia sent out by AMPs made contact with surrounding muscles (Figure 1D-G' and Video 1) and by embryonic stage 16 had become tightly associated with neighboring muscles.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1D-G' and Video 1.

claim: Lateral AMPs extend from the external to internal muscle layer.
source: We observed that AMPs associate with several rather than just one particular muscle layer. For example, the lateral AMPs extend from the external to internal layer.
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by Videos 2 and 3.

claim: Lateral AMPs send out filopodia non-randomly and mainly in anterior-dorsal directions, which correlate with the location of SBM and LO/LT muscles.
source: We focused on lateral AMPs and found that they send out filopodia non-randomly and mainly in anterior-dorsal directions, which correlate with the location of SBM and LO/LT muscles to which lateral AMPs are connected.
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by Video 4.

claim: Some filopodia of AMPs stabilize during the homing period.
source: Thus, the filopodia are projected mainly in the direction of targeted muscles, ultimately enabling a subset of them to stabilize (arrowheads in Video 4).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Video 4.

claim: There is plasticity in AMP-muscle interactions, as demonstrated by reaper-induced muscle ablation experiments.
source: However, reaper-induced muscle ablation experiments (Figure 2A–D) revealed that there is some plasticity in AMP-muscle interactions.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2A-D showing muscle ablation experiments.

claim: Dorsal-ventral positional information restricts AMP–muscle contacts.
source: This finding indicates that dorsal-ventral positional information restricts AMP–muscle contacts.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that dorsal AMPs could not connect to lateral muscles in ablation experiments (Figure 2B).

claim: AMP cell loss correlates with the severity of muscle ablation phenotypes.
source: Moreover, we observed AMP cell loss (asterisks in Figure 2) correlating with the severity of muscle ablation phenotypes (compare Figure 2B,C and D), which suggests that AMP interactions with muscles are important for their survival.
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B-D.

claim: AMP interactions with muscles are important for AMP survival.
source: Moreover, we observed AMP cell loss (asterisks in Figure 2) correlating with the severity of muscle ablation phenotypes (compare Figure 2B,C and D), which suggests that AMP interactions with muscles are important for their survival.
evidence: This inference is drawn from the correlation between muscle ablation and AMP loss shown in Figure 2.

claim: The first α-PS1 punctate signals associated with AMPs appear at late-stage 14.
source: The first α-PS1 punctate signals associated with the AMP cell body appear at late-stage 14 (arrowhead, Figure 2E,E') and are progressively enriched at stages 15 and 16 (Figure 2F,G', Videos 5 and 6).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2E,E'.

claim: α-PS1 integrin is progressively enriched at AMP-muscle contacts at stages 15 and 16.
source: The first α-PS1 punctate signals associated with the AMP cell body appear at late-stage 14 (arrowhead, Figure 2E,E') and are progressively enriched at stages 15 and 16 (Figure 2F,G', Videos 5 and 6).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figures 2F,G' and Videos 5 and 6.

claim: Punctate α-PS1 patterns are associated with AMP cell bodies and aligned with filopodia.
source: Punctate α-PS1 patterns were associated mainly with the AMP cell bodies (arrowheads in Figure 2F,G', Videos 5 and 6) but were also seen to be aligned with filopodia (arrows in Figure 2F,G', Videos 5 and 6).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figures 2F,G' and Videos 5 and 6.

claim: β-PS integrin dots are detected from stage 15 at AMP-muscle contacts.
source: Similarly distributed but more discrete β-PS dots were also detected from stage 15 (Figure 2H,H').
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2H,H'.

claim: Integrins mark filopodia subsets that are making contact with target muscles and in the process of stabilization.
source: As filopodia are highly dynamic structures, we posit that integrins mark filopodia subsets that are making contact with target muscles and in the process of stabilization.
evidence: This hypothesis is stated in the text and supported by observations of integrin localization and filopodia dynamics.

claim: The interconnecting cellular processes of AMPs are present in first-instar larvae but are progressively lost and become undetectable in second instar larvae.
source: We found that the interconnecting cellular processes are present in first-instar larval AMPs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) but are then progressively lost, becoming undetectable in second instar larvae (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and 1B.

claim: The filopodia- and cell body-based contacts of AMPs with neighboring muscles persist along larval life until AMP reactivation.
source: However, the filopodia- and cell body-based contacts of AMPs with neighboring muscles persist along larval life until AMP reactivation (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: Quiescent AMPs at early second larval instar project relatively few filopodia compared to late embryonic stage.
source: Compared with the late embryonic stage (Figure 3A), quiescent AMPs at early second larval instar (Figure 2B) project relatively few filopodia.
evidence: This comparison is stated in the text and supported by Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: At early second larval instar, lateral AMPs adopt highly elongated shapes with two long cellular protrusions that extend and follow growing muscle.
source: As shown for lateral AMPs (Figure 3B), they adopt highly elongated shapes with two long cellular protrusions that extend and follow growing muscle.
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: At early second larval instar, lateral AMPs restrict their contact to the two closest muscle neighbors, SBM and LO1.
source: At this stage, the lateral AMPs restrict their contact to the two closest muscle neighbors, i.e. SBM and LO1, illustrating preferential interactions with these two muscles already seen in embryos.
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3B.

claim: AMPs maintain elongated shapes with long cellular extensions aligning neighboring muscles until the beginning of their reactivation.
source: The observation that the AMPs maintain elongated shapes with long cellular extensions aligning neighboring muscles until the beginning of their reactivation (Figure 3C) suggests that the association of AMPs with muscle niche could play a role in their exit from the quiescent state.
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: After a few rounds of proliferation, AMPs adopt more rounded shapes but stay closely associated to each other and to the muscle niche.
source: After a few rounds of proliferation, AMPs adopt more rounded shapes (Figure 3D) but stay closely associated to each other and to the muscle niche (Figure 3D).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The exit of neuroblasts from the dormant state is subject to a nutritional checkpoint involving the TOR pathway.
source: The progenitors of the fly brain, the neuroblasts, also behave quiescently during development, and it has been reported that their exit from the dormant state is subject to a nutritional checkpoint involving the TOR pathway and that glial cell-derived Insulin signals are required to initiate their proliferation (Chell and Brand, 2010, Sousa-Nunes et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Chell and Brand, 2010, and Sousa-Nunes et al., 2011.

claim: Glial cell-derived Insulin signals are required to initiate neuroblast proliferation.
source: The progenitors of the fly brain, the neuroblasts, also behave quiescently during development, and it has been reported that their exit from the dormant state is subject to a nutritional checkpoint involving the TOR pathway and that glial cell-derived Insulin signals are required to initiate their proliferation (Chell and Brand, 2010, Sousa-Nunes et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Chell and Brand, 2010, and Sousa-Nunes et al., 2011.

claim: AMPs stay quiescent in third-instar larvae growing in nutrient-restricted conditions.
source: We observed that AMPs stay quiescently in third-instar larvae growing in nutrient-restricted conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that similar mechanisms could also drive their reactivation.
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: AMP-targeted expression of PTEN results in dramatically lower numbers of AMPs.
source: The AMP-targeted expression of PTEN, which negatively regulates Insulin signaling or TOR inhibitors (TSC1, TSC2), results in dramatically lower numbers of AMPs (Figure 4B,E,J, Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4B,E,J and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: AMP-targeted expression of TOR inhibitors (TSC1, TSC2) results in dramatically lower numbers of AMPs.
source: The AMP-targeted expression of PTEN, which negatively regulates Insulin signaling or TOR inhibitors (TSC1, TSC2), results in dramatically lower numbers of AMPs (Figure 4B,E,J, Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4E,J and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Overexpression of InRCA (constitutively activated form of Insulin receptor) results in higher numbers of AMPs.
source: Conversely, we found higher numbers of AMPs following the overexpression of InRCA, a constitutively activated form of the Insulin receptor, or Rheb, the positive modulator of the TOR pathway (Figure 4D,J, Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4C,J and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Overexpression of Rheb (positive modulator of TOR pathway) results in higher numbers of AMPs.
source: Conversely, we found higher numbers of AMPs following the overexpression of InRCA, a constitutively activated form of the Insulin receptor, or Rheb, the positive modulator of the TOR pathway (Figure 4D,J, Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4D,J and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Insulin/TOR pathway components are not sufficient to drive AMP exit from quiescence in embryonic stages.
source: However, these same components were not sufficient to drive AMP exit from quiescence in the embryonic stages (Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—source data 1) and only managed to accelerate AMP entry into proliferation from the mid to early second larval instar.
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Insulin/TOR pathway activation accelerates AMP entry into proliferation from the mid to early second larval instar.
source: However, these same components were not sufficient to drive AMP exit from quiescence in the embryonic stages (Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—source data 1) and only managed to accelerate AMP entry into proliferation from the mid to early second larval instar.
evidence: This observation is stated in the text.

claim: Insulin/TOR pathways are part of a more complex regulatory cascade driving the reactivation of dormant AMPs in a developmental time-window restricted to mid-larval stages.
source: This suggests that Insulin/TOR pathways are part of a more complex regulatory cascade driving the reactivation of dormant AMPs in a developmental time-window restricted to mid-larval stages.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that Insulin/TOR activation is not sufficient in embryos.

claim: A regulatory element of Enhancer of split m6 (E(spl)m6; m6) gene carries potential Supressor of Hairless (Su(H)) binding sites.
source: We previously reported that a regulatory element of Enhancer of split m6 (E(spl)m6; m6) gene carrying potential Supressor of Hairless (Su (H)) binding sites (Rebeiz et al., 2002) drives expression specifically in quiescent AMPs (Figeac et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations to Rebeiz et al., 2002 and Figeac et al., 2010.

claim: The m6 regulatory element drives expression specifically in quiescent AMPs.
source: We previously reported that a regulatory element of Enhancer of split m6 (E(spl)m6; m6) gene carrying potential Supressor of Hairless (Su (H)) binding sites (Rebeiz et al., 2002) drives expression specifically in quiescent AMPs (Figeac et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation to Figeac et al., 2010.

claim: m6-Gal4-targeted expression of NICD in embryonic AMPs does not alter their quiescence in embryos.
source: Here, we showed that m6-Gal4-targeted expression of the Notch intracellular domain (NICD) in embryonic AMPs does not alter their quiescence in embryos (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: NICD expression results in significantly higher numbers of AMPs in third-instar larvae.
source: However, in the same NICD context, there were significantly higher numbers of AMPs in third-instar larvae, suggesting that Notch reactivates AMPs in larval stages and promotes their proliferation (Figure 4F,J, Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4F,J and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Notch reactivates AMPs in larval stages and promotes their proliferation.
source: However, in the same NICD context, there were significantly higher numbers of AMPs in third-instar larvae, suggesting that Notch reactivates AMPs in larval stages and promotes their proliferation (Figure 4F,J, Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation of increased AMP numbers with NICD expression.

claim: Reduced number of AMPs in larvae with m6-driven Notch attenuation supports the role of Notch in AMP proliferation.
source: The reduced number of AMPs in larvae with m6-driven Notch attenuation (Figure 4G,J, Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—source data 1) further supports this observation.
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4G,J and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: In vertebrate satellite cells, Notch regulates asymmetric divisions controlling the number of reserve muscle stem cells.
source: In vertebrate satellite cells, Notch regulates the asymmetric divisions controlling the number of reserve muscle stem cells that, at the end of the cell cycle, sit on muscles and remain undifferentiated (Kuang et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Kuang et al., 2007.

claim: Activated AMPs do not divide asymmetrically.
source: The activated AMPs do not seem to divide asymmetrically, as they did not increase in number in the numb RNAi context (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and no reactivated AMPs were found to express the asymmetric cell division marker Numb-CD2-GFP (Rebeiz et al., 2011) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from numb RNAi experiments and Numb-CD2-GFP expression analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Notch plays a novel role in AMPs, promoting their proliferation without driving asymmetric cell divisions.
source: Notch thus plays a novel role in AMPs, promoting their proliferation without driving asymmetric cell divisions.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that AMPs do not divide asymmetrically but Notch promotes their proliferation.

claim: In vertebrates, the transcription factor Myc is involved in regulating myoblast proliferation during muscle development and regeneration.
source: Besides the Insulin and Notch pathways, a recent study (Li et al., 2012) found that in vertebrates the transcription factor Myc is also involved in regulating myoblast proliferation during muscle development and regeneration.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Li et al., 2012.

claim: dMyc acts as a positive regulator of AMP reactivation.
source: Indeed, dMyc acts as a positive regulator of AMP reactivation (Figure 4H–K, Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—source data 1), thus providing evidence that the proliferation of muscle stem cells is regulated by the same set of genes in both Drosophila and vertebrates.
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4H-K and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The proliferation of muscle stem cells is regulated by the same set of genes in both Drosophila and vertebrates.
source: Indeed, dMyc acts as a positive regulator of AMP reactivation (Figure 4H–K, Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—source data 1), thus providing evidence that the proliferation of muscle stem cells is regulated by the same set of genes in both Drosophila and vertebrates.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that dMyc regulates AMP proliferation, similar to its role in vertebrates.

claim: t-PGH protein binds specifically to phosphatidylinositol-3,4,5-P3 (PIP3) and, if localized to plasma membrane, indicates PI3K/Insulin pathway activity.
source: It has been reported that the plekstrin homology (PH) domain containing t-PGH protein binds specifically to phosphatidylinositol-3,4,5-P3 (PIP3) and, if localized to plasma membrane, indicates PI3K/Insulin pathway activity (Britton et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Britton et al., 2002.

claim: t-PGH is specifically recruited to plasma membrane in AMPs that undergo cell divisions.
source: The data show that t-PGH is specifically recruited to plasma membrane in AMPs that undergo cell divisions (Figure 5A- A" and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5A-A" and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Proliferating AMPs display high levels of intracellular Notch and nuclear dMyc.
source: Importantly, the proliferating AMPs also display high levels of intracellular Notch and nuclear dMyc (Figure 5B–B''), showing that activation of the Insulin pathway and increased Notch and dMyc levels correlate with the reactivated AMPs state.
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5B-B''.

claim: Activation of the Insulin pathway and increased Notch and dMyc levels correlate with the reactivated AMPs state.
source: Importantly, the proliferating AMPs also display high levels of intracellular Notch and nuclear dMyc (Figure 5B–B''), showing that activation of the Insulin pathway and increased Notch and dMyc levels correlate with the reactivated AMPs state.
evidence: This correlation is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: The mean fluorescent intensity representing Notch and dMyc protein levels is increased in the InRCA context compared with wild-type.
source: First, we quantified the level of Notch and dMyc in the individual lateral AMPs, and found that the mean fluorescent intensity representing Notch and dMyc protein levels was increased in the InRCA context (Figure 5C,C",J,K and Figure 5—source data 1) compared with wild-type (Figure 5B,B'',J,K and Figure 5—source data 1) and was significantly lower in the AMPs expressing the negative regulator of Insulin signaling PTEN (Figure 5J,K and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5C,C",J,K.

claim: Notch and dMyc protein levels are significantly lower in AMPs expressing PTEN.
source: First, we quantified the level of Notch and dMyc in the individual lateral AMPs, and found that the mean fluorescent intensity representing Notch and dMyc protein levels was increased in the InRCA context (Figure 5C,C",J,K and Figure 5—source data 1) compared with wild-type (Figure 5B,B'',J,K and Figure 5—source data 1) and was significantly lower in the AMPs expressing the negative regulator of Insulin signaling PTEN (Figure 5J,K and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5J,K.

claim: The Insulin pathway positively regulates Notch and dMyc during AMP reactivation.
source: The Insulin pathway thus positively regulates Notch and dMyc during AMP reactivation.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that InRCA increases Notch and dMyc levels while PTEN decreases them.

claim: Notch increases nuclear dMyc levels in AMPs.
source: Next, using the same approach, we tested dMyc protein levels in AMP-targeted gain and loss of Notch function, and found that Notch increased nuclear dMyc levels (Figure 5D,D'', Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5—source data 1), suggesting that Notch acts upstream of dMyc.
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5D,D'' and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Notch acts upstream of dMyc during AMP reactivation.
source: Next, using the same approach, we tested dMyc protein levels in AMP-targeted gain and loss of Notch function, and found that Notch increased nuclear dMyc levels (Figure 5D,D'', Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5—source data 1), suggesting that Notch acts upstream of dMyc.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that Notch increases dMyc levels.

claim: Lowering Notch or dMyc levels in AMPs expressing InRCA leads to an attenuation of the AMP overproliferation phenotype.
source: We found that lowering Notch or dMyc levels in AMPs expressing InRCA led to an attenuation of the AMP overproliferation phenotype, indicating that both Notch and dMyc act downstream of the Insulin pathway (Figure 5E–G,L, M, Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5E-G,L,M and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both Notch and dMyc act downstream of the Insulin pathway during AMP proliferation.
source: We found that lowering Notch or dMyc levels in AMPs expressing InRCA led to an attenuation of the AMP overproliferation phenotype, indicating that both Notch and dMyc act downstream of the Insulin pathway (Figure 5E–G,L, M, Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from genetic rescue experiments shown in Figure 5E-G,L,M.

claim: The increased number of AMPs generated in the NICD-overexpressing context is dMyc-dependent.
source: We also observed that the increased number of AMPs generated in the NICD-overexpressing context was dMyc-dependent (Figure 5H,I,L, M, Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5—source data 1), indicating that dMyc acts as an effector of Notch in reactivated AMPs.
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5H,I,L,M and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: dMyc acts as an effector of Notch in reactivated AMPs.
source: We also observed that the increased number of AMPs generated in the NICD-overexpressing context was dMyc-dependent (Figure 5H,I,L, M, Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5—source data 1), indicating that dMyc acts as an effector of Notch in reactivated AMPs.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that dMyc attenuation rescues NICD overproliferation.

claim: An Insulin-Notch-dMyc cascade governs the exit of AMPs from the dormant state and promotes their proliferation.
source: Taken together, these data establish an Insulin-Notch-dMyc cascade governing the exit of AMPs from the dormant state and promoting their proliferation (Figure 5M).
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the genetic epistasis experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: NICD overexpression induces higher numbers of AMPs than InRCA overexpression.
source: However, as NICD overexpression induces higher numbers of AMPs than InRCA overexpression (Figure 5L, Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5—source data 1), we cannot rule out the possibility that Notch also acts in an InR-independent way.
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5L and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Notch may also act in an InR-independent way during AMP proliferation.
source: However, as NICD overexpression induces higher numbers of AMPs than InRCA overexpression (Figure 5L, Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5—source data 1), we cannot rule out the possibility that Notch also acts in an InR-independent way.
evidence: This possibility is raised based on the observation that NICD has a stronger effect than InRCA.

claim: Knocking down Delta or Serrate in muscle or PNS cells has no effect on AMP proliferation.
source: We thus tested whether the attenuation of Delta or Serrate in the muscle or PNS cells with which AMPs are associated impacts on AMP proliferation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Figure 6—source data 1). We found that knocking down Notch ligands in direct AMP cell neighbors has no effect on AMP reactivation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Expressing a dominant-negative form of Notch receptor (ECN) in AMPs has no effect on AMP cell numbers.
source: Similarly, expressing in AMPs a dominant-negative form of Notch receptor (ECN) devoid of intracellular domain and known to efficiently repress canonical Notch signaling (Rebay et al., 1993) had no effect on AMP cell numbers (Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Figure 6—source data 1), suggesting that Notch activation in AMPs could occur in a ligand-independent way.
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Notch activation in AMPs could occur in a ligand-independent way.
source: Similarly, expressing in AMPs a dominant-negative form of Notch receptor (ECN) devoid of intracellular domain and known to efficiently repress canonical Notch signaling (Rebay et al., 1993) had no effect on AMP cell numbers (Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Figure 6—source data 1), suggesting that Notch activation in AMPs could occur in a ligand-independent way.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that blocking canonical Notch signaling does not affect AMP proliferation.

claim: Deltex plays a role in ligand-independent intracellular activation of Notch by promoting its mono-ubiquitinated state.
source: To further explore the Insulin-Notch pathway linkage, we tested the expression of the ubiquitin ligase Deltex, which is known to play a role in ligand-independent intracellular activation of Notch by promoting its mono-ubiquitinated state (Hori et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Hori et al., 2011.

claim: Punctate cytoplasmic Deltex expression increases significantly in AMPs expressing InRCA compared to control.
source: We found that punctate cytoplasmic Deltex expression increased significantly in AMPs expressing InRCA compared to the control (Figure 6A–C and Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6A-C.

claim: Targeted expression of Deltex in AMPs leads to an overproliferation phenotype.
source: Consistently with this observation, targeted expression of Deltex in AMPs or attenuation of its repressor Supressor of Deltex (Su (Dx)) both led to an overproliferation phenotype (Figure 6D,E,I and Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6D,E,I.

claim: Attenuation of Supressor of Deltex (Su(Dx)) in AMPs leads to an overproliferation phenotype.
source: Consistently with this observation, targeted expression of Deltex in AMPs or attenuation of its repressor Supressor of Deltex (Su (Dx)) both led to an overproliferation phenotype (Figure 6D,E,I and Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6E,I.

claim: Non-visual β-arrestin homolog Kurtz (Krz) binds together with Deltex to the Notch receptor, leading to its poly-ubiquitination and subsequent degradation.
source: Hori et al. (2011) proposed that non-visual β-arrestin homolog Kurtz (Krz) binds together with Deltex to the Notch receptor, leading to its poly-ubiquitination and subsequent degradation.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Hori et al., 2011.

claim: Both increasing and decreasing Kurtz levels leads to overproliferation of AMPs.
source: We tested Krz function in AMPs and found that both increasing and decreasing Kurtz levels leads to overproliferation of AMPs (Figure 6—figure supplement 2 and Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The stoichiometry of Krz and Dx levels regulates Notch activation in AMPs.
source: This suggested that the stoichiometry of Krz and Dx levels regulates Notch activation in AMPs (see schemes in Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that both increasing and decreasing Kurtz leads to overproliferation.

claim: Reducing Deltex by RNAi-based attenuation leads to an increased number of AMPs.
source: Indeed, reducing Deltex by RNAi-based attenuation or by overexpressing Su (Dx) led to an increased number of AMPs (Figure 6—figure supplement 2 and Figure 6-source data 1) similar to that observed in the Deltex overexpression context (Figure 6D,I and Figure 6—source data 1), whereas simultaneous overexpression of Deltex and Kurtz had no effect on AMP numbers (Figure 6—figure supplement 2 and Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Simultaneous overexpression of Deltex and Kurtz has no effect on AMP numbers.
source: Indeed, reducing Deltex by RNAi-based attenuation or by overexpressing Su (Dx) led to an increased number of AMPs (Figure 6—figure supplement 2 and Figure 6-source data 1) similar to that observed in the Deltex overexpression context (Figure 6D,I and Figure 6—source data 1), whereas simultaneous overexpression of Deltex and Kurtz had no effect on AMP numbers (Figure 6—figure supplement 2 and Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Shrub, a component of the ESCRT-III complex, promotes Notch degradation in multivesicular bodies (MVBs) and acts as a negative regulator of ligand-independent Notch activity.
source: It has also been reported that Shrub, a component of the ESCRT-III complex that promotes Notch degradation in multivesicular bodies (MVBs), acts as a negative regulator of ligand-independent Notch activity (Hori et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Hori et al., 2011.

claim: Downregulation of Shrub in AMP cells results in a burst of AMP proliferation.
source: We found that a downregulation of Shrub in AMP cells results in a burst of AMP proliferation (Figure 6F,I and Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6F,I.

claim: Overexpressing Deltex or Kurtz in InRCA context increases AMP cell numbers compared to InRCA alone.
source: Consistent with all these data, overexpressing Deltex or Kurtz in InRCA context increased AMP cell numbers compared to InRCA alone (Figure 6G,I, Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6G,I and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Overexpressing Deltex in AMPs in which the Insulin pathway was attenuated by PTEN restores AMP proliferation back up to wild-type levels.
source: On the other hand, overexpressing Deltex in AMPs in which the Insulin pathway was attenuated by PTEN restored AMP proliferation back up to wild-type levels (Figure 6H,I and Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6H,I.

claim: During AMP reactivation, the Insulin pathway activates Notch in a Deltex and Shrub-involving ligand-independent way.
source: Taken together, this body of evidence suggests that during AMP reactivation, the Insulin pathway activates Notch in a Deltex and Shrub-involving ligand-independent way.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the genetic experiments showing Deltex and Shrub involvement in Notch activation downstream of Insulin.

claim: AMP proliferation is only inhibited in a dIlp6 loss-of-function background, not in dIlp2 or dIlp5 mutants.
source: We first tested mutants for dIlp2, dIlp5 and dIlp6 (Grönke et al., 2010) and found that AMP proliferation was only inhibited in a dIlp6 loss-of-function background (Figure 7A–C,J, Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7A-C,J and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Blocking secretion from larval muscles by expressing Shi-DN affects the proliferation of AMPs and reduces their numbers.
source: We found that blocking the secretion from larval muscles affected the proliferation of AMPs and reduced their numbers (Figure 7D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Figure 7—source data 1), whereas no effect was observed when Shi-DN was expressed in either neural cells (Figure 7E,J, Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Figure 7—source data 1) or glial cells (Figure 7F,J, Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Expressing Shi-DN in neural cells or glial cells has no effect on AMP proliferation.
source: We found that blocking the secretion from larval muscles affected the proliferation of AMPs and reduced their numbers (Figure 7D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Figure 7—source data 1), whereas no effect was observed when Shi-DN was expressed in either neural cells (Figure 7E,J, Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Figure 7—source data 1) or glial cells (Figure 7F,J, Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7E,F,J and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Attenuating dIlp6 expression in muscles reduces AMP numbers.
source: A key role of muscles in producing dIlp6 and inducing AMP proliferation is further supported by the reduction of AMP numbers in larvae with attenuated dIlp6 expression in muscles but not in glial cells (Figure 7G,I,J, Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7G,J and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Attenuating dIlp6 expression in glial cells does not affect AMP numbers.
source: A key role of muscles in producing dIlp6 and inducing AMP proliferation is further supported by the reduction of AMP numbers in larvae with attenuated dIlp6 expression in muscles but not in glial cells (Figure 7G,I,J, Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7I,J and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Muscle-specific overexpression of dIlp6 results in an increased number of AMPs.
source: Conversely, an increased number of AMPs was detected in muscle-specific overexpression of dIlp6 (Figure 7H,J, Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7H,J and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: DAAM-attenuation leads to altered AMP proliferation in third-instar larvae.
source: We found that DAAM-attenuation leads to an altered AMP proliferation in third-instar larvae (Figure 7M and Figure 7—source data 1) that correlates with reduced length of cellular protrusions observed in DAAM-RNAi second-instar larvae (Figure 7L, compare to wild-type shown in Figure 7K).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7M.

claim: DAAM-attenuation correlates with reduced length of cellular protrusions in second-instar larvae.
source: We found that DAAM-attenuation leads to an altered AMP proliferation in third-instar larvae (Figure 7M and Figure 7—source data 1) that correlates with reduced length of cellular protrusions observed in DAAM-RNAi second-instar larvae (Figure 7L, compare to wild-type shown in Figure 7K).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7L compared to 7K.

claim: Muscle appears to be the source of local inductive Insulin signals that reactivate AMPs.
source: Thus, like for satellite cells (Chakkalakal et al., 2012), muscle appears to play a niche role while also proving essential to the activation of quiescent AMPs (Figure 8).
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the genetic experiments showing muscle-derived dIlp6 is required for AMP reactivation.

claim: Direct contact between AMPs and surrounding muscles via long cellular protrusions promotes the reception of local, muscle-derived dIlp6 by the closely-associated AMPs.
source: On the other hand, the lack of substantial effect on AMP proliferation observed in dIlp2, dIlp3 and dIlp5 mutants suggests that dIlps secreted to the hemolymph are unable to reactivate AMPs and that direct contact between AMPs and surrounding muscles via long cellular protrusions promotes the reception of local, muscle-derived dIlp6 by the closely-associated AMPs.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that only dIlp6 affects AMP proliferation and AMPs maintain contact with muscles.

claim: Muscle plays a niche role and is essential to the activation of quiescent AMPs.
source: Thus, like for satellite cells (Chakkalakal et al., 2012), muscle appears to play a niche role while also proving essential to the activation of quiescent AMPs (Figure 8).
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observations of AMP-muscle interactions and muscle-derived dIlp6 requirement.

claim: Numerous IGF signaling components are upregulated in activated satellite cells.
source: Whether the Insulin/IGF signals play a conserved role in this process remains an open question, but the finding that numerous IGF signaling components are upregulated in activated satellite cells (Pallafacchina et al., 2010) argues for this possibility.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Pallafacchina et al., 2010.

claim: AMPs are similar to vertebrate satellite cells based on their capacity to send out cytoplasmic extensions and make interconnections.
source: Interestingly, the capacity to send out cytoplasmic extensions and make interconnections has also been documented for quiescent satellite cells sited on myofibers (Tavi et al., 2010). All these features make AMPs similar to vertebrate satellite cells, prompting us to analyze their homing behavior and the mechanisms that drive their activation and exit from the dormant state.
evidence: This comparison is stated in the text and supported by citation to Tavi et al., 2010.

claim: The niche of satellite cells is composed of cellular and extracellular components (muscle fiber and basal lamina) that are sufficient for satellite cell activation, proliferation and differentiation.
source: The niche of satellite cells located underneath the basal lamina of myofibers is composed of cellular and extracellular components (muscle fiber and basal lamina) that are sufficient for satellite cell activation, proliferation and differentiation (Zammit et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Zammit et al., 2004.

claim: Niche properties, particularly of its muscle component, are crucial for the regenerative potential of satellite cells during aging.
source: Niche properties, particularly of its muscle component, also appear crucial for the regenerative potential of satellite cells during aging (Chakkalakal et al., 2012) and satellite cell engraftment in cell therapy approaches (Boldrin et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Chakkalakal et al., 2012.

claim: AMPs lie at the origin of all adult Drosophila muscles.
source: The stem-like Drosophila AMPs specified in mid-embryogenesis lie at the origin of all the adult Drosophila muscles (Bate et al., 1991), but the lack of appropriate genetic tools means we still know little of their behavior and niche requirements.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Bate et al., 1991.

claim: Quiescent stem cells have few mitochondria and use anaerobic metabolism.
source: Quiescent stem cells have few mitochondria and use anaerobic metabolism, whereas activated cells switch their metabolism to a high ATP energy output aerobic glycolysis in order to support the high-level macromolecular synthesis required for proliferation, (Montarras et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Montarras et al., 2013.

claim: Activated stem cells switch their metabolism to a high ATP energy output aerobic glycolysis to support high-level macromolecular synthesis required for proliferation.
source: Quiescent stem cells have few mitochondria and use anaerobic metabolism, whereas activated cells switch their metabolism to a high ATP energy output aerobic glycolysis in order to support the high-level macromolecular synthesis required for proliferation, (Montarras et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Montarras et al., 2013.

claim: Genes encoding glycolytic and pyruvate metabolic enzymes known to be downstream of Insulin act as upstream regulators of the Notch pathway.
source: Interestingly, genes encoding glycolytic and pyruvate metabolic enzymes known to be downstream of Insulin (Tixier et al., 2013) act as upstream regulators of the Notch pathway (Saj et al., 2010), providing a potential link between metabolism and Notch in regulating the quiescent versus activated state of stem cells.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Tixier et al., 2013 and Saj et al., 2010.

claim: Quiescent non-differentiated cells keep Notch activated.
source: A well-known feature of quiescent non-differentiated cells is that they keep Notch activated (Bjornson et al., 2012), but Notch receptor activation can also trigger proliferation (Baonza and Garcia-Bellido, 2000), including the proliferation of satellite cells (Qin et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Bjornson et al., 2012.

claim: Notch receptor activation can trigger proliferation, including the proliferation of satellite cells.
source: A well-known feature of quiescent non-differentiated cells is that they keep Notch activated (Bjornson et al., 2012), but Notch receptor activation can also trigger proliferation (Baonza and Garcia-Bellido, 2000), including the proliferation of satellite cells (Qin et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Baonza and Garcia-Bellido, 2000, and Qin et al., 2013.

claim: Notch regulates the proliferation of cancer cells via Myc.
source: As Notch regulates the proliferation of cancer cells via Myc (Palomero et al., 2006; Weng et al., 2006; Liao et al., 2007; Ishikawa et al., 2013), and Myc promotes the proliferation of myoblasts during development and regeneration (Li et al., 2012), we tested whether dMyc was involved in AMP reactivation in Drosophila.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Palomero et al., 2006; Weng et al., 2006; Liao et al., 2007; Ishikawa et al., 2013.

claim: Coordinated activation of Insulin and Notch pathways regulates the self-renewal and differentiation of intestinal Drosophila stem cells.
source: Interestingly, it has been shown that coordinated activation of Insulin and Notch pathways also regulates the self-renewal and differentiation of intestinal Drosophila stem cells (Foronda et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Foronda et al., 2014.

claim: The role of ligand-independent Notch activation, which involves interaction with Hif-α, is essential for normal Drosophila blood cell development.
source: The role of ligand-independent Notch activation, which involves interaction with Hif-α, has been reported as essential for normal Drosophila blood cell development (Mukherjee et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Mukherjee et al., 2011.

claim: Three Insulin-like peptides (dIlp2, dIlp3 and dIlp5) secreted to the hemolymph by mNSC cells control the systemic growth of the organism.
source: In Drosophila, three Insulin-like peptides (dIlp2, dIlp3 and dIlp5) secreted to the hemolymph by mNSC cells control the systemic growth of the organism (Brogiolo et al., 2001), whereas dIlp6 produced by the glial cells acts locally and promotes the proliferation of the neuroblasts (Sousa-Nunes et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Brogiolo et al., 2001.

claim: dIlp6 produced by glial cells acts locally and promotes the proliferation of neuroblasts.
source: In Drosophila, three Insulin-like peptides (dIlp2, dIlp3 and dIlp5) secreted to the hemolymph by mNSC cells control the systemic growth of the organism (Brogiolo et al., 2001), whereas dIlp6 produced by the glial cells acts locally and promotes the proliferation of the neuroblasts (Sousa-Nunes et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Sousa-Nunes et al., 2011.
